title: A song for the Sabbath (Psalm 92)
hookLine: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree"

lines: A SABBATH SONG THAT NEVER SAYS SABBATH.
cards: Friday evening. The candles are lit. In the synagogue, people have been singing psalms to welcome Shabbat, one after another.
Then comes a particular one, and in many communities, that's the moment Shabbat is taken on. The work is done. The psalm announces itself in its first line: a song for the Sabbath day.
And then, strangely, it never mentions the Sabbath again.

teach.b: It begins: "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day." In Hebrew, mizmor shir le-yom ha-Shabbat. It's the Levites' song for Shabbat from the Temple, said on Friday night and again on Shabbat morning.
Then it gets going: it's good to give thanks to the Lord, to tell of His kindness in the morning and His faithfulness in the night.
And not a word about rest, candles or the seventh day. So why is this the Sabbath psalm? The rabbis gave answers.
The Mishnah ends its list of daily psalms by calling this one a song for the time to come, a day that will be entirely Sabbath and rest. A midrash puts it in the mouth of Adam himself.

And some readers say it's about what Shabbat lets a person see. During the week, there's no time to notice that the wicked spring up like grass and don't last. On Shabbat, there's time to stop and see what does.
Then the well-known line: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon." Two trees.
The palm, with its sweet fruit.
The cedar, tall and strong and lasting. Some commentators say you need both: sweetness and strength. And these trees, the psalm adds, still bear fruit in old age, full of sap and green.
That closes a week of psalms: what is man, the shepherd, clean hands, Ashrei, a psalm for each day, Hallel, and today, the Sabbath song.

how: Psalm 92 is said during Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday evening, often marking the moment the congregation accepts Shabbat, and again on Shabbat morning as the Song of the Day.

games.q: a psalm calls itself a song for the Sabbath, but never mentions the Sabbath again. how did the Mishnah explain it?
o: it's a song for the time to come, a day that is all Sabbath.
it was meant for a weekday.
games.why: the Mishnah (Tamid 7:4) calls it a song for the time to come, a day entirely Sabbath and rest.

practice: Whatever day it is, you can taste Shabbat: put down your work for two minutes, even in your mind, and hum a gentle tune, any tune, or the niggun from a few weeks ago.

As you hum, picture a palm, tall and sweet with fruit, then a cedar, deep-rooted and strong, and ask: where am I sweet, where am I strong? If it's Shabbat where you are, let this be part of it, and if you pray, give thanks.

wordCard.voice: Mizmor, Hebrew for a psalm, the word that opens Psalm ninety-two: a song for the Sabbath, sung as Shabbat arrives. The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like the cedar, bearing fruit even in old age.
